Yevhen Petrenko · obstetrician-gynecologist, Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)
25 years in obstetrics. I provide antenatal care, attend births, teach doctors and talk to parents-to-be about pregnancy — evidence-based and without fear.
Preconception care, antenatal care, birth and the postpartum period — respecting your choices and grounded in evidence-based medicine.
Postgraduate education, caesarean section training (basic and advanced), teaching guidelines for residents.

400 mcg daily from at least one month before conception until 12 weeks of pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects in the baby.
Your doctor will review chronic conditions and medicines. Some drugs (such as valproate or isotretinoin) must be switched before conception.
Live vaccines (rubella, measles, chickenpox) are not given during pregnancy. After such a vaccine it is advisable to wait one month before conceiving.
A normal weight before pregnancy lowers the risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia and complications during birth.
No smoking — for both of you
Smoking harms fertility and fetal development. Second-hand smoke matters too, so both partners should quit.
Alcohol: there is no safe amount
Alcohol can cause harm even before you know you are pregnant. The safest choice is to stop while you are planning a pregnancy.
Well-controlled diabetes, hypertension or thyroid disease before conception substantially lowers the risks for mother and baby.
WHO recommends 250 mcg of iodine a day for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Ukraine is an iodine-deficient region — discuss this with your doctor.
After a birth, WHO advises waiting at least 24 months before the next conception — this lowers the risks for both mother and baby.
Regular visits help detect complications early. They are also time for all your questions — even the awkward ones.
One ultrasound scan before 24 weeks confirms gestational age and the number of babies and helps detect anomalies.
WHO recommends daily iron with folic acid throughout pregnancy. Your doctor will choose the dose.
No extra calories are needed in the first trimester; about 340 extra kcal a day in the second and about 450 in the third.
It depends on your weight before pregnancy. For a woman with a normal BMI — about 11.5–16 kg over the whole pregnancy.
Up to 200 mg of caffeine a day, roughly two cups. Caffeine is also found in tea, cola and chocolate.
Fish — yes, but the right kind
2–3 servings a week of low-mercury fish (salmon, hake, cod). Avoid shark, swordfish and king mackerel.
Avoid raw or undercooked meat, raw eggs and unpasteurised milk — this protects against listeriosis and toxoplasmosis.
Without contraindications, about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is recommended: walking, swimming, pregnancy yoga.
The flu vaccine can be given at any stage of pregnancy, the whooping cough vaccine at 27–36 weeks. The protection passes to the baby.
Dental check-ups and treatment during pregnancy are safe. Gum inflammation should be treated, not put off.
Women at high risk of pre-eclampsia may be prescribed low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks. Do not start it on your own.
Severe headache, flashing lights or spots in front of the eyes, sudden swelling of the face or hands — see a doctor immediately.
In the third trimester, sleep on your side
After 28 weeks, go to sleep on your left or right side rather than on your back. If you wake up on your back, simply turn over.
Pay attention to your baby's movements
If your baby is moving less than usual or the pattern of movements has changed, seek care straight away — don't wait until morning.
The lap belt goes below your bump, across your hips; the shoulder belt goes between your breasts. The belt protects both you and your baby.
In an uncomplicated pregnancy, flying is usually fine until 36 weeks. On the way, move around often and drink water.
In an uncomplicated pregnancy, sex is safe. Restrictions apply only to certain conditions — your doctor will tell you.
Anxiety or low mood during pregnancy are common. Tell your doctor — help exists and it works.
A birth companion of your choice
Support from a partner or another close person helps you feel calmer — this is a WHO recommendation.
Skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping (no earlier than 1 minute) and the first breastfeed within the first hour.
